scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that lets interest lead while refusing to ignore job prospects; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Students often feel pulled between studying what they love and studying what will pay the bills.
Some people recommend that colleges encourage students to pursue subjects that interest them rather than courses that seem most likely to lead to jobs.
I agree that interest should guide students more than fear of the job market, but I believe job prospects cannot be ignored completely.
First, students usually learn best and achieve most when they study something they genuinely care about.
Interest brings the energy and persistence that carry a student through difficult and demanding work.
For example, a student fascinated by history will read, think, and write far more deeply than one who chose a subject only for money.
This shows that real passion often produces better results than a reluctant pursuit of a merely safe career.
People who follow their genuine interests are also more likely to find lasting satisfaction in their working lives.
Successful careers, moreover, often grow out of a deep enthusiasm that began as a simple personal interest.
For these reasons, interest deserves to play the leading role in a student's choice.
Second, however, encouraging interest should not mean ignoring the practical question of employment.
A graduate with deep knowledge but no way to earn a living may find that her passion turns quickly into worry.
Consider a talented student who studies a beloved subject with no job prospects, then struggles for years under heavy debt.
Such hardship can slowly drain the very joy that made the subject worth choosing in the first place.
Colleges therefore do students a service by helping them connect their interests to realistic career paths.
Many fields, after all, allow a student to follow a passion while still building useful and employable skills.
Encouraging interest works best when it is paired with honest advice about the future.
In conclusion, colleges are right to encourage students to follow subjects that truly interest them.
But they should also help students keep an eye on the job prospects that will support those interests.
The best guidance lets passion lead the way while making sure students can still earn a decent living.
